oracle_docs.a_conviction_score_is_a_probabilistic_cl: A conviction score is a probabilistic claim, and a probabilistic claim is worthless unless it's checked against reality. Oracle joins every verdict to its ground-truth outcome and publishes the result on the page — including when the edge is thin. This is the part that separates a model from a vibe.

oracle_docs.a_high_score_is_the_weight_of: A high score is the weight of on-chain evidence, not a guarantee. pump.fun is adversarial and heavy-tailed — most launches fail, and even a calibrated edge loses often. Read the tier as odds, size accordingly, and never bet what you can't lose.
oracle_docs.a_long_lived_node_process_running_three: A long-lived Node process running three independent loops — score (keep verdicts warm), agent (act on armed watches), and settle (grade outcomes) — each self-scheduling so a slow pass never blocks a fast one.
oracle_docs.a_model_you_can_only_trust_when: A model you can only trust when it flatters you is useless. Here is what Oracle cannot do, where it can be wrong, and how it's hardened.

oracle_docs.a_pure_side_effect_free_scoring_function: A pure, side-effect-free scoring function (convict()) plus a defensive data-assembly layer. Given a mint, it returns a score, tier, pillar breakdown, and reasons. No I/O during scoring — fully testable.
oracle_docs.a_scored_coin_is_a_win_if: A scored coin is a win if it graduated, or reached a ≥2× ATH multiple without rugging; a loss if it rugged or languished below 1.2×; flat in between. The "without rugging" clause matters: bundled launches routinely spike 2× from first sight before collapsing, and counting those wicks as wins would let pump-and-dumps inflate the very number that's supposed to expose them. Only resolved coins count toward a win rate — open positions are excluded, so the number can't be inflated by undecided bets.
oracle_docs.a_single_long_lived_node_process_runs: A single long-lived Node process runs three independent, self-scheduling loops. They share nothing but the database, so a slow scoring pass never delays an agent acting, and a stuck confirmation never freezes scoring.

oracle_docs.oracle_reads_every_pump_fun_launch_the: Oracle reads every pump.fun launch the moment it appears and answers one question: how much conviction does the on-chain evidence actually support? It fuses four independent reads — who is buying, how the launch is structured, what story it rides, and how it is moving — into a single transparent 0–100 score, then lets your 3D agent act on the plays that clear your bar. This is the complete reference: the thesis, the exact math, the data, the evidence, the API, the limits, and where it goes next.
oracle_docs.oracle_reads_from_a_separate_full_covera: Oracle reads from a separate full-coverage data brain rather than touching the chain itself. The brain ingests pump.fun and maintains the reputation graph; Oracle assembles, classifies, and fuses. The separation is what keeps scoring a pure, fast function.
oracle_docs.oracle_s_wager_is_that_a_transparent: Oracle's wager is that a transparent, calibrated fusion of who / how / what / move beats both gut instinct and any single indicator, because the failure modes are independent. A great story (WHAT) cannot save a launch where the dev already sold (HOW). A pile of smart-money wallets (WHO) means little if they are already trimming (also WHO). Fusing independent reads cancels noise and surfaces the rare launch where every axis agrees.

oracle_docs.plain_english_drivers_buyers_strongly_ou: Plain-English drivers: buyers strongly outnumbering sellers, a rapid pile-in of unique early buyers, and a dev who put a sensible amount of skin in the game all lift the score. Heavy early selling cuts it, and an oversized dev buy is read as a honeypot risk and penalized.
oracle_docs.plain_english_drivers_each_category_carr: Plain-English drivers: each category carries a prior (how durable that kind of story tends to be), and the model's virality estimate is blended with that prior, weighted by the model's own confidence. A confidently-viral culture coin scores high; an unclassifiable one is treated with caution. It's the lightest pillar on purpose — a story is a multiplier on a real launch, not a substitute for one.
oracle_docs.plain_english_drivers_many_unique_early_: Plain-English drivers: many unique early buyers and low concentration push the score up. Bundles, a top wallet holding half the supply, 70% of volume sniped in the first seconds, armies of freshly-funded wallets, or a dev who already sold all push it down — and the worst of these cap the whole coin in the 38–55 range regardless of pedigree.
oracle_docs.plain_english_drivers_more_proven_wallet: Plain-English drivers: more proven wallets in is better; a large share of the buy volume coming from proven money is better; a creator who has shipped graduated launches before is better. Conversely, flagged wallets, smart money already selling, and a creator with a rug pattern all cut the score — and a serial rugger caps it outright.

New evasion patterns are caught by the outcome loop (they rug, reputation updates) before they're caught by a rule. The defense is the closed loop, not any single check.

oracle_docs.the_proven_wins_gallery_ordered_by_ath: The proven-wins gallery, ordered by ATH multiple, with a summary.
oracle_docs.the_question_is_real_buying_pressure_act: The question: is real buying pressure actually showing up, right now? Momentum reads the earliest footprint — the buy/sell balance, how fast unique buyers are piling in, and the size of the dev's own buy as a tell.
oracle_docs.the_question_is_this_a_fair_launch: The question: is this a fair launch or an engineered one? Structure is the guardrail. It reads the distribution and timing of the launch — bundle likelihood, holder concentration, snipe pressure, fresh-wallet farming, single-funder clusters, dev selling — and rewards broad, organic bases while punishing coordination and concentration.
oracle_docs.the_question_what_is_this_coin_about: The question: what is this coin about, and does the story have cultural legs? Narrative classifies the launch into one of eleven categories (meme, ai, culture, news, animal, celebrity, political, community, tech, utility, unknown) and estimates its virality — preferentially with a language model that is given live crypto headlines so it can recognize a coin riding today's news.
oracle_docs.the_question_who_is_already_in_this: The question: who is already in this coin, and what is their record? Pedigree rewards launches where wallets with a proven history of getting into winners early are already buying — and penalizes the presence of known ruggers, dumpers, and serial failed-launch creators.
oracle_docs.the_scoring_is_a_pure_function_of: The scoring is a pure function of assembled intel. Everything stateful — ingestion, persistence, execution, settlement — lives outside it. That boundary is why the math is testable, the verdicts are reproducible, and the same engine powers the live feed, the API, and an agent's decision with identical results.
oracle_docs.the_snapshot_above_is_a_thin_low: The snapshot above is a thin, low-conviction window — realized win rates sit below the band midpoints and few coins reached the higher tiers. That is shown, not hidden. The page is built to display a weak edge as readily as a strong one, because a backtest you only trust when it flatters you isn't a backtest.
oracle_docs.the_system_gets_sharper_the_more_it: The system gets sharper the more it watches, on two flywheels. The data flywheel: every resolved outcome updates the wallet-reputation graph that powers the WHO pillar, so the definition of "smart money" is continuously re-earned, never hard-coded. The calibration flywheel: every graded outcome tightens the backtest, exposing exactly where the score is over- or under-confident so the model can be re-weighted against reality rather than intuition.
oracle_docs.the_what_pillar_depends_on_a_language: The WHAT pillar depends on a language model and a news feed; both can misread a story or miss a fast-breaking one. It's the lightest-weighted pillar for exactly this reason, and it degrades to a deterministic classifier rather than failing.
oracle_docs.the_what_pillar_is_the_only_place: The WHAT pillar is the only place Oracle reaches outside the brain. To classify a launch's story, it fetches live crypto headlines from a public news API (cached ~90s), injects them into the language model's prompt, and asks for a category, a one-line narrative, a virality estimate, and a confidence. A coin literally riding today's headline gets recognized as such and scored higher. If the model is unavailable, a deterministic keyword classifier takes over so a verdict always ships.

oracle_docs.the_worker_is_configured_entirely_by_env: The worker is configured entirely by environment. Live mode additionally requires the secret used to decrypt agent wallets, and refuses to start without it.

oracle_docs.two_coins_can_both_score_70_for: Two coins can both score 70 for completely different reasons — one on pure pedigree with weak momentum, another on a viral narrative over a thin base. The tier tells you how strong; the reasons tell you why, and the why is what you trade on.

oracle_docs.two_win_rates_are_published_deliberately: Two win rates are published, deliberately kept apart: the call win rate (resolved coins Oracle rated Lean, Strong, or Prime — the tiers it tells you to act on) and the market base rate (every scored launch — what blindly buying everything would return). Until real calls resolve, the call win rate reads "no calls resolved yet"; the base rate is never presented as the engine's skill.
oracle_docs.unlike_the_normal_approximation_the_wils: Unlike the normal approximation p ± z·√(p(1−p)/n), the Wilson interval stays inside [0,1], doesn't collapse to zero width at p=0 or p=1, and behaves correctly for the small n that young backtests have. It is the difference between an honest "we don't know yet" and a dishonest "0% ± 0%."
oracle_docs.walking_the_drawer_top_to_bottom_mirrors: Walking the drawer top to bottom mirrors the model exactly:
oracle_docs.weighted_average_of_the_four_pillar_scor: # weighted average of the four pillar scores
oracle_docs.when_a_coin_launches_the_people_who: When a coin launches, the people who win are the ones who already know things you can't see fast enough: whose wallets are buying (and whether those wallets have a track record or a rug history), whether the launch is organic or a coordinated bundle, whether the "community" is 200 real people or 200 freshly-funded burner wallets, and whether the story has cultural legs. By the time a human reads a chart, the asymmetry has already paid out.
oracle_docs.when_a_coin_s_outcome_resolves_the: When a coin's outcome resolves, the settle loop grades any open action on it:
oracle_docs.who_and_how_together_carry_nearly_two: WHO and HOW together carry nearly two-thirds of the weight because who is buying and how fair the launch is are the two facts that most reliably separate runners from rugs. WHAT and MOVE are lighter — they break ties and confirm, but a good story or a green first minute can't rescue a coin the harder pillars condemn.
oracle_docs.who_s_in_is_the_live_pedigree: Who's-in is the live pedigree roster — every notable wallet, its label, and its track record.
oracle_docs.why_this_score_is_the_array_each: “Why this score” is the reasons[] array, each line tagged to the pillar that generated it. In this example: "no proven wallets identified yet" (WHO), "clean, distributed launch structure" (HOW), "meme narrative, virality 45/100" (WHAT), "no clear momentum yet — too early" (MOVE). A clean-but-unproven young launch — correctly a watch, not an avoid and not a buy.
oracle_docs.wilson_1927_probable_inference_the_law_o: Wilson (1927), Probable inference, the law of succession, and statistical inference — the score interval. Brier (1950), Verification of forecasts expressed in terms of probability. Platt (1999), probabilistic outputs for SVMs (Platt scaling). Zadrozny & Elkan (2002), isotonic calibration. Niculescu-Mizil & Caruana (2005), Predicting good probabilities with supervised learning.
oracle_docs.wilson_interval_the_95_score_interval_on: Wilson interval: the 95% score interval on each tier/bin win rate (derivation in the evidence deep-dive), correct for small n and bounded to [0,1].
oracle_docs.win_loss_isn_t_known_until_a: Win/loss isn't known until a coin resolves, so the backtest always trails the present. Recent windows are thin and their confidence bands are wide — and the page shows the width rather than hiding it.
oracle_docs.win_rate_by_tier_with_honest_error: Win rate by tier, with honest error bars
oracle_docs.win_rate_by_tier_with_wilson_cis: Win rate by tier with Wilson CIs, calibration ladder, Brier, and the edge summary. Filters: period, tier, network.
oracle_docs.win_the_coin_graduated_or_its_peak: Win — the coin graduated, or its peak multiple reached ≥2× on a coin that didn't rug and isn't marked below half entry.
oracle_docs.with_no_signal_yet_it_returns_too: With no signal yet it returns "too early," keeping the pillar neutral rather than inventing momentum that isn't there.

three_ws_launch_week.beyond_the_analytics_dashboard_three_ws_: Beyond the analytics dashboard, three.ws landed on the directories, registries, and platforms that matter most for an open-source developer tool.
three_ws_launch_week.elevenlabs_voice_cloning_from_3_10_secon: ElevenLabs voice cloning from 3–10 seconds of speech, persona extraction from a short onboarding interview, and consented memory seeding from connected accounts — the avatar isn’t just you, the agent acts like you.

three_ws_launch_week.meta_og_description: Open-source 3D AI agent platform for the browser. Week one in numbers and what we shipped.
three_ws_launch_week.meta_twitter_description: Everything three.ws shipped during launch week — 3D avatars, agent payments, the x402 bazaar, and more.
three_ws_launch_week.open_source_3d_ai_agent_platform_apache: Open-source 3D AI agent platform. Apache 2.0. Built with three.js, Claude, and a belief that AI deserves a body.
three_ws_launch_week.pulled_directly_from_x_analytics_for_try: Pulled directly from X analytics for @trythreews between April 29 and May 9. No filtering, no averaging tricks — the headline numbers below and the charts further down come from the same screenshot.
three_ws_launch_week.reputation_markets_staking_on_agents_sig: Reputation markets staking on agents’ signed action histories, EIP-7710 skill royalties paid to skill authors per-call, and agent-to-agent autonomous payments through delegated signer wallets.
three_ws_launch_week.the_custom_element_loads_lazily_on_inter: The <agent-3d> custom element loads lazily on intersection, supports five widget variants (turntable, animation gallery, talking agent, ERC-8004 passport card, hotspot tour), and emits Open Graph and oEmbed metadata so links unfurl with rich previews. A point-and-click Widget Studio generates copy-paste embed code at /studio. Versioned CDN bundles ship at /agent-3d/x.y.z/.
three_ws_launch_week.the_google_cloud_announcement_was_the_si: The Google Cloud announcement was the single highest-engagement post of the week (~6.9K impressions, 263 likes, 24 reposts) and the cloud infrastructure backing the next phase of the platform.
three_ws_launch_week.the_inside_the_3d_agent_web_podcast: The “Inside The 3D Agent Web” podcast episode is published on Amazon Music and the companion blog “Beyond Chatbots: Why Your AI Agent Needs a 3D Body” went out via the Spotify-on-chain ecosystem. Two more distribution surfaces, one more week.
three_ws_launch_week.the_platform_shipped_as_a_partner_listin: The platform shipped as a partner listing on Alibaba Cloud, our first cloud-marketplace distribution channel. The associated launch tweet pulled ~7.1K impressions on its own.
three_ws_launch_week.the_roadmap_closes_the_gap_from_use: The roadmap closes the gap from “use a 3D artist” to “take a selfie”. Four phases, scoped end-to-end in the public README.
three_ws_launch_week.the_runtime_drives_a_claude_tool_loop: The runtime drives a Claude tool-loop with up to eight iterations per turn and six built-in tools (wave, lookAt, play_clip, setExpression, speak, remember). The Empathy Layer is not a state machine — it’s a continuous weighted blend of five emotions (celebration, concern, curiosity, empathy, patience), each with its own decay half-life, driving the avatar’s morph targets and head pose every frame. Skills are self-contained bundles distributable over IPFS, Arweave, or HTTP. Memory is file-based with four storage modes (local, IPFS, encrypted-IPFS, none).
three_ws_launch_week.the_three_ws_x_community_is_the: The three.ws X community is the gathered audience — developers, agent-curious builders, and a crew of folks following along live. It’s where the next wave of agent owners will come from.
three_ws_launch_week.three_selfies_left_center_right_gpu_back: Three selfies (left, center, right), GPU-backed multi-view face reconstruction, and a rigged, animatable avatar minted as a draft ERC-8004 token in under sixty seconds. Mobile-first capture UX with realtime quality gates.
three_ws_launch_week.three_solidity_contracts_make_up_the_erc: Three Solidity contracts make up the ERC-8004 implementation: IdentityRegistry (ERC-721 agent tokens with delegated EIP-712 signers), ReputationRegistry (signed reviewer feedback, averaged on-chain), and ValidationRegistry (validator attestations for off-chain proofs). Every speak, remember, and skill-done event is signed and logged. Solana ships an analog using Metaplex Core NFTs plus signed SPL Memo attestations — same shape, no custom program required.
three_ws_launch_week.three_ws_is_an_open_source_browser: three.ws is an open-source, browser-native 3D AI agent platform. We shipped the full stack — viewer, agent runtime, on-chain identity, OAuth 2.1 server, MCP endpoint, and an embeddable web component — then watched the launch land. Here’s what happened.
three_ws_launch_week.three_ws_is_organized_as_four_communicat: three.ws is organized as four communicating layers, plus a backend and a contracts package. Every layer is in production at three.ws and ships as part of the open-source repo. Here’s the inventory.
three_ws_launch_week.three_ws_is_published_as_on_registry: three.ws is published as io.github.nirholas/three.ws on registry.modelcontextprotocol.io and discoverable via PulseMCP’s curated directory. Any MCP-aware client (Claude Desktop included) can connect and drive avatars over JSON-RPC.
three_ws_launch_week.vercel_functions_on_neon_postgres_cloudf: Vercel functions on Neon Postgres, Cloudflare R2, and Upstash Redis. A full OAuth 2.1 server (RFC 6749 + PKCE, RFC 7591 dynamic registration, RFC 7009 revocation, RFC 7662 introspection, RFC 8414 discovery, RFC 9728 protected-resource discovery). An MCP server over HTTP — 759 lines, JSON-RPC 2.0, listed on the official Model Context Protocol Registry as io.github.nirholas/three.ws. Cron jobs for the ERC-8004 crawler, EIP-7710 delegation indexer, DCA strategy execution, and recurring on-chain subscriptions.
three_ws_launch_week.webgl_2_0_rendering_with_full_gltf: WebGL 2.0 rendering with full glTF 2.0 / GLB support: Draco geometry compression, KTX2 texture compression, Meshopt mesh optimization, HDR environment maps, PBR materials, skinned animation, morph targets, and embedded cameras. Validation is line-level via the Khronos gltf-validator. Drag-and-drop loading, OrbitControls with configurable auto-rotation, and a real-time dat.GUI for live tweaking.
three_ws_launch_week.webgl_viewer_llm_agent_runtime_erc_8004: WebGL viewer, LLM agent runtime, ERC-8004 identity contracts, OAuth 2.1 server, MCP endpoint, and the <agent-3d> web component — everything you read about above. Live at three.ws today.
